title: Missing Number
statement: A list holds n different numbers, all taken from 0 to n. That range has n + 1 values, so exactly one is absent. Find the absent number. Aim for one pass and constant extra memory.

example.caption: The range is 0 to 3. The list has 3, 0, 1, so 2 is missing.

idea.sentence: XOR every index 0..n with every value in the list. Each present number cancels with itself, and the missing one is left over.

jargon.plain: Compares two numbers bit by bit. The result bit is 1 only where the two bits differ. x ^ x is 0.
A position in the list, counted from 0. Together with the values it covers each number in 0..n once as an index and once as a value.

vars.meaning: length of the list (the range is 0..n)

compare.bruteLabel: For each value 0..n, scan the list

rows.name: Search each value
rows.note: For every value in 0..n, scan the list to see if it is there.

rows.name: Hash set
rows.note: Put the numbers in a set, then probe 0..n.

rows.name: XOR indexes and values
rows.note: One pass, one integer. Pairs cancel and the gap stays.

rows.name: Sum formula
rows.note: n(n+1)/2 minus the sum of the list. Same cost. Risks overflow in fixed-width ints for huge n.

fast.takeaway: XOR and the sum formula both cost one pass and no memory. XOR never overflows, because the result stays inside the bits of the inputs.

stages.title: Start at n
stages.note: x starts as the list length. n is an index that never appears as a position (positions stop at n - 1).

stages.title: XOR index and value
stages.note: x ^= i ^ nums[i]. Each present number cancels itself, once as index and once as value.

stages.title: Return x
stages.note: Only the missing number was never cancelled.

edges.title: n is missing
edges.why: Every index 0 and 1 cancels a value. Only the start value x = n = 2 survives, which is why x does not start at 0.

edges.title: Zero is missing
edges.why: Range 0..1. x = 1, then 1 ^ 0 ^ 1 = 0. A 0 answer is real, not a no-answer signal.

edges.title: Only zero present
edges.why: The one-number list is missing n itself.

edges.title: Shuffled order
edges.why: XOR does not care about order, so the list does not need sorting.

gotchas.text: Start x at n, not at 0. The loop covers indexes 0 to n - 1, so without the start value the number n can never cancel, and a list that misses n returns the wrong answer.
Bitwise operators convert to signed 32-bit integers. List values are far below 2^31, so XOR is safe. A value of 2^31 or more would wrap silently.
The sum formula is exact in JS up to 2^53, so it also works. Go's int is 64-bit and holds n(n+1)/2 easily, but a 32-bit int (int32) can overflow for n above about 65,000.
i ^ v is XOR here because it sits between two values. ^x with one operand is bitwise NOT. Mixing them up is a quiet bug.

recap.key: Fold in every index and every value. All numbers present appear twice and cancel. The missing one appears only as an index.
moves: For each i, x ^= i ^ nums[i]
